'''Richard A. Glennon''' is an [[American people|American]] [[medicinal chemist]] who studies [[psychedelic drug|psychedelic]]s, [[stimulant]]s, [[entactogen]]s, and other [[psychoactive drug]]s.<ref name="Geyer2024">{{cite journal | vauthors = Geyer MA | title = A Brief Historical Overview of Psychedelic Research | journal = Biol Psychiatry Cogn Neurosci Neuroimaging | volume = 9 | issue = 5 | pages = 464–471 | date = May 2024 | pmid = 38000715 | doi = 10.1016/j.bpsc.2023.11.003 | url = | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="FordyceRoth2024">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fordyce BA, Roth BL | title = Making Sense of Psychedelics in the CNS | journal = Int J Neuropsychopharmacol | volume = 27 | issue = 2 | pages = | date = February 2024 | pmid = 38289825 | pmc = 10888522 | doi = 10.1093/ijnp/pyae007 | url = | quote = In 1983, Richard Glennon and colleagues identified psychedelic-induced behaviors by mescaline and LSD that were subsequently blocked by antagonists ketanserin and pirenperone in rats (Glennon et al., 1983a). From this, serotonin (5-HT) 5-HT2 receptors were suspected as primary contributors to these affects. [...] In 1983, Glennon and colleagues provided an in-depth review of the [drug discrimination (DD) paradigm, referencing numerous studies using the DD paradigm to assess both interoceptive cues and relative potencies of different psychoactive compounds (Glennon et al., 1983b). }}</ref><ref name="PellerinSeefeltCrumb1998">{{cite book | last1=Pellerin | first1=C. | last2=Seefelt | first2=E. | last3=Crumb | first3=R. | title=Trips: How Hallucinogens Work in Your Brain | publisher=Seven Stories Press | year=1998 | isbn=978-1-888363-34-0 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ux08WPnfb-UC&pg=PA81 | access-date=5 February 2025 | pages=9, 81–85, 112}}</ref><ref name="CameronJohnsonMurnane2026">{{cite journal | last1=Cameron | first1=Lindsay P. | last2=Johnson | first2=Matthew W. | last3=Murnane | first3=Kevin S. | last4=Rasenick | first4=Mark M. | last5=Nichols | first5=Charles D. | title=Next-Generation Psychedelic Drug Development | journal=ACS Chemical Neuroscience | date=15 September 2026 | issn=1948-7193 | doi=10.1021/acschemneuro.6c00492 | url=https://pubs.acs.org/acncdm/article/doi/10.1021/acschemneuro.6c00492/5429719/Next-Generation-Psychedelic-Drug-Development | access-date=19 September 2026 | quote=Another chemist who played a prominent role in the early chemistry of psychedelics is Dr. Richard Glennon, who spent his career at Virginia Commonwealth University. In addition to synthesizing many new 5-HT2A51 ligands, he published in 1984 a study demonstrating that the affinity of ligands for the 5-HT2 receptor had a strong positive correlation with behavioral effects, thus demonstrating that the receptor target of psychedelics was the 5-HT2 receptor.52| doi-access=free }}</ref> He has been an important pioneer of the use of animal [[drug discrimination]] tests in [[scientific research]] for studying psychoactive drugs like [[hallucinogen]]s.<ref name="Nichols2004">{{cite journal | vauthors = Nichols DE | title = Hallucinogens | journal = Pharmacol Ther | volume = 101 | issue = 2 | pages = 131–181 | date = February 2004 | pmid = 14761703 | doi = 10.1016/j.pharmthera.2003.11.002 | url = | quote = Table 1 gives a comparison of human dosages for several compounds where drug discrimination data in LSD-trained rats also have been obtained from the author’s laboratory. Although there are several other hallucinogens that have been characterized using the drug discrimination paradigm, particularly by Richard Glennon and his colleagues, different training drugs have been used. [...] The earliest hypothesis that hallucinogenic drugs acted specifically at 5-HT2 receptor subtypes was proposed by Glennon et al. (1983c) based on drug discrimination studies in rats showing that the 5-HT2 antagonists ketanserin and pirenperone blocked the discriminative stimulus effects of phenethylamine and tryptamine hallucinogens, including LSD (Colpaert et al., 1982; Leysen et al., 1982; Colpaert & Janssen, 1983). Earlier studies (Browne & Ho, 1975; Winter, 1975) had also shown that the discriminative stimulus of mescaline was blocked by 5-HT antagonists that later were recognized to block 5-HT2 receptors. }}</ref><ref name="FordyceRoth2024" /><ref name="PellerinSeefeltCrumb1998" /> Glennon has also done a large amount of work on the [[structure–activity relationship]]s of psychedelics.<ref name="CameronJohnsonMurnane2026" /><ref name="Olson2021">{{cite journal | vauthors = Olson DE | title = The Promise of Psychedelic Science | journal = ACS Pharmacol Transl Sci | volume = 4 | issue = 2 | pages = 413–415 | date = April 2021 | pmid = 33860170 | pmc = 8033768 | doi = 10.1021/acsptsci.1c00071 | url = | quote = Collectively, the SAR studies in this issue add to the large body of work by David Nichols, Richard Glennon, and others, investigating how the structures of psychedelics lead to their hallucinogenic effects.6−8 }}</ref> In addition, he played an important role in the discovery that the hallucinogenic effects of psychedelics are mediated by activation of [[serotonin]] [[5-HT2 receptor|5-HT<sub>2</sub> receptor]]s.<ref name="CameronJohnsonMurnane2026" /><ref name="Nichols2004" /><ref name="FordyceRoth2024" /><ref name="López-GiménezGonzález-Maeso2018">{{cite book | vauthors = López-Giménez JF, González-Maeso J | title = Behavioral Neurobiology of Psychedelic Drugs | chapter = Hallucinogens and Serotonin 5-HT2A Receptor-Mediated Signaling Pathways | series = Current Topics in Behavioral Neurosciences | volume = 36 | pages = 45–73 | date = 2018 | pmid = 28677096 | pmc = 5756147 | doi = 10.1007/7854_2017_478 | isbn = 978-3-662-55878-2 | chapter-url = | quote = The role of the 5-HT2A receptor in the mechanism of action of hallucinogens was first proposed by Richard Glennon, Milt Titeler and their teams (Glennon et al. 1984, 1986). However, it was not until the development of 5-HT2A knockout mice in 2003 that the fundamental role of 5-HT2A receptor-dependent signaling in the cellular and behavioral effects of hallucinogens was verified conclusively (Gonzalez-Maeso et al. 2003 2007). }}</ref><ref name="Jacobs1987">{{cite journal | last=Jacobs | first=Barry L. | title=How Hallucinogenic Drugs Work: Hallucinogenic drugs appear to exert their effects by acting on a specific type of serotonin receptor in the brain | journal=American Scientist | publisher=Sigma Xi, The Scientific Research Society | volume=75 | issue=4 | year=1987 | issn=0003-0996 | jstor=27854718 | pages=386–392 | url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/27854718 | access-date=5 February 2025}}</ref> He is one of the most widely cited scientists in his field.<ref name="Komornik2024">{{cite web | last=Komornik | first=Emily | title=New listing of the world's most-cited scientists includes 11 VCU faculty | website=School Of Pharmacy | date=31 October 2024 | url=https://pharmacy.vcu.edu/news/newsroom/pharmacy-news/new-listing-of-the-worlds-most-cited-scientists-includes-glennon-10-other-vcu-faculty-who-rank-in-the-top-50-of-their-fields.html | access-date=5 February 2025}}</ref> Glennon was the [[editor-in-chief]] of the [[scientific journal|journal]] ''[[Medicinal Chemistry Research]]'' from 1992 to 2002.<ref name="JonesDukat2022">{{cite web | last1=Jones | first1=Charles B. | last2=Dukat | first2=Małgorzata | title=Special Issue in honor of former Editor-in-Chief Prof. Richard Glennon | website=SpringerLink | date=3 March 2022 | url=https://link.springer.com/collections/fccdcifjjc | access-date=5 February 2025}}</ref> He retired in 2022 but has continued to publish reviews and research since then.<ref name="JonesDukat2022" />
